summary: Defines a method for negotiating data encryption over PPP links. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers on a link agree on whether to scramble the messages and which scrambler to use.

questions: what is the ppp encryption control protocol
what ppp protocol value is used for encrypted datagrams
subtitle: How the two ends of a PPP link agree to encrypt their traffic, and which cipher to use.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry traffic over a point-to-point link, but it has no built-in way for the two ends to agree on encrypting that traffic or on which encryption algorithm to use.
tldr.mechanism: The Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) reuses the LCP packet machinery to negotiate one algorithm per direction, then encrypted data travels in PPP frames marked with their own protocol value. Reset-Request and Reset-Ack packets recover from decryption failures.
tldr.outcome: Links can protect themselves against eavesdropping with an algorithm both ends accept, including vendor-specific ones. The RFC notes that complete security can only come from end-to-end security between hosts.

today: RFC 1968 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PPP Needs an Encryption Protocol
sections.content:
Before a PPP link carries data, each end sends Link Control Protocol (LCP) packets to configure and test the link. After the link is established, optional facilities can be negotiated as needed. RFC 1968 defines one such facility: data encryption.

A wide variety of encryption methods may be negotiated, although typically only one method is used in each direction. The two directions can use different algorithms, for speed, cost, memory or other considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two friends pass notes, they can agree to write them in a secret code. This RFC is the rule book for agreeing on the code, and each friend may even pick a different one.

sections.title: ECP: LCP With a Few Changes
sections.content:
The Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) configures and enables encryption algorithms at both ends of the link. It uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP and is exactly the same as LCP except for a few points.

  • An ECP packet travels in the PPP Information field, and the PPP Protocol field is hex 8053. For individual link encryption in a multiple link connection, it is hex 8055.
  • ECP uses codes 1 through 7 (Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject), and may also use codes 14 and 15. Other codes should be treated as unrecognised and answered with Code-Rejects.
  • ECP has its own set of Configuration Options.

ECP packets may not be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and packets received earlier should be silently discarded. An implementation should be ready to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before timing out. An implementation MUST NOT transmit data until ECP negotiation has completed successfully, and if it fails the link SHOULD be brought down.
sections.plainLanguage: ECP is the same polite conversation the link already uses, just about codes instead of settings. Nobody may send secret messages until both have agreed on the code.

sections.title: Sending Encrypted Datagrams
sections.content:
Encrypted packets can flow only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase and ECP reaches the Opened state. An encrypted packet goes in the PPP Information field with the PPP Protocol field set to hex 0053 (Encrypted datagram). The protocol value says the frame is encrypted but not which algorithm was used, so only one algorithm per direction can be in use at a time.

With multiple PPP links to one destination there are two methods. Either encrypt the data before sending it out over the links, using protocol 0053, or treat each link as a separate connection. On links that negotiated encryption in the second method, the protocol field MUST be hex 0055 (Individual link encrypted datagram).

An encrypted packet can be no longer than the Information field of a PPP packet allows. If the algorithm is likely to make a message bigger, multilink should also be negotiated so frames can be fragmented, even over a single link. If the algorithm carries history between frames, it must let the ends tell whether data is passing reliably, or require a reliable transport such as LAPB.

When compression is also negotiated, plain text MUST be compressed first and then encrypted. The RFC chose this order because it should give smaller output and more secure encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypted messages get a special stamp on the envelope that says secret inside, but not which code. If a message might grow when scrambled, you need to be able to split it up. Squash it small first, then scramble it.

sections.title: Recovering With Reset-Request and Reset-Ack
sections.content:
ECP adds two codes to LCP's set: 14 (Reset-Request) and 15 (Reset-Ack). They let one end signal a decryption failure in one direction without disturbing traffic in the other. Some algorithms may not need them, and each algorithm must specify how to detect a decryption failure.

On first detecting a failure, an implementation SHOULD send a Reset-Request. The Data field may hold any desired data. After sending one, it discards any encrypted packets it receives. It may resend with the same Identifier until a valid Reset-Ack arrives, but sending more often than the link's round-trip time only causes redundant packets. The receiver MAY limit itself to something like one per second while a Reset-Ack is outstanding.

When a Reset-Request arrives, the transmitting encrypter is reset to an initial state and a Reset-Ack MUST be sent, copying the Identifier from the request. When a Reset-Ack arrives, the receiving decrypter is reset to an initial state. Because several Reset-Acks may be in flight, the decrypter MUST be reset for each one that matches the currently expected identifier.

Both packets have the same layout as an LCP packet: Code, Identifier, Length, then Data. The Identifier MUST change whenever the Data content changes and after a valid reply to a previous request, and SHOULD stay the same on retransmissions. Data can be any length from zero up to the peer's established MRU minus four.
sections.plainLanguage: If a scrambled message turns into gibberish, the receiver shouts reset. The sender starts its scrambler over from the beginning and says okay, and then both are back in step.

sections.title: ECP Configuration Options
sections.content:
ECP uses the same Configuration Option format as LCP, with a separate set of options. An option names an algorithm the receiver is willing or able to use to decrypt data from the sender. The option types assigned at the time of writing are 0 for OUI and 1 for DESE. All compliant implementations SHOULD implement option 1, the PPP DES Encryption Protocol (RFC 1969).

Proprietary encryption uses option type 0, which carries an IEEE Organisationally Unique Identifier (OUI), the first three octets of a vendor's Ethernet address. The length is at least 6. A Subtype field is specific to each OUI and not standardised, followed by optional vendor Values. Vendors can use this without asking IANA for an option number. Since the first matching encryption is used, known OUI options should be sent first, and an implementation must check that it can decrypt the algorithm and understands the vendor values before accepting.

Publicly available types use option type 1 to 254 with a length of at least 2 followed by algorithm-specific Values. These protocols should be made available to interested parties but may have licencing or export restrictions. All options other than OUI are registered by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each option is a card saying I can read this kind of secret code. Companies can make up their own cards using their company number, and shared codes get official numbers.

sections.title: Negotiating an Algorithm
sections.content:
ECP uses LCP option negotiation, but unlike most other negotiation it is expected to converge on a single option, or none. Encryption SHOULD be negotiated in both directions, though the algorithms MAY differ.

The end willing to decrypt is the Decrypter and its peer is the Encrypter. The Decrypter sends a Configure-Request with either an ordered list of options, most preferred first, or just its preferred option that has not been rejected.

  • To accept the first-listed algorithm, the Encrypter MAY Configure-Ack all options.
  • If it does not recognise or will not support an option, it MUST Configure-Reject it, and SHOULD reject all but one preferred option when several are offered.
  • If it recognises an option but the values are unacceptable, it MUST send a Configure-Nak with the option modified, containing only acceptable options. The Decrypter SHOULD then send a new request with only that single option, adjusted as the Nak says.
  • If the Encrypter rejects every option and the Decrypter has nothing else to offer, the Encrypter SHOULD take the link down.
sections.plainLanguage: One side lists the codes it can read, favourite first. The other side picks one it also knows, or says none of those. If they cannot agree on anything, they hang up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Negotiating encryption over PPP is designed to protect against eavesdropping on that one link. How strong the protection is depends on the algorithm used and on how carefully any secret that algorithm uses is protected.

The RFC adds that complete security can only be obtained through end-to-end security between hosts. Link encryption does not cover the rest of the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Scrambling the notes only protects them while they cross one hallway. To be really safe, they have to stay scrambled all the way to the person who reads them.
